title: Burst from one address

why: A single address hitting the firewall, sshd or fail2ban many times in a minute is a scan or a brute-force run. ALM raises this one error instead of letting the individual lines bury it.

title: Lost the link to myserver
what: ALM's connection to myserver dropped, and it is retrying with growing delays up to a minute.
why: ALM reads myserver's logs over ssh. The link drops when myserver or the network goes down, or when this machine wakes from sleep. Entries missed during the gap are backfilled from the journal.

title: Asset load
what: {who} fetched {path} (a font, image or script that a page needs) from {ip}.
why: The browser loads these after a page view. ALM normally folds them into the view, so seeing one alone is unusual.

title: Probe redirected
what: {who} asked for {path}, a path scanners look for, and Caddy answered with a redirect (HTTP {status}) instead of the page.
why: A 308 here is most likely the plain-http to https redirect, so the probe never reached an application. Many probes from one address is a scan, and ALM flags it.

title: Probe for a missing path
what: {who} requested {path} and got HTTP {status}. The path does not exist or is not allowed.
why: Scanners look for well-known paths such as /.env, /wp-login.php and /admin. Each 404 is a miss. Many from one address is a scan, and ALM flags it.

title: CONNECT request redirected
what: {who} sent a CONNECT request for {path}, which is how a client asks a server to act as a proxy. Caddy redirected it (HTTP {status}).
why: Open-proxy scanners send CONNECT to every web server they find. Caddy does not proxy for strangers, so nothing was relayed.

title: POST redirected
what: {who} sent a POST to {path} and Caddy redirected it (HTTP {status}).
why: Bots POST to login and form endpoints. A redirect means the request was bounced before reaching any app.

title: Page view
what: {who} loaded the page {path} from {ip}.
why: Caddy, the web server, logs every request. ALM turns each line into a sentence and folds the fonts and images that follow a page view into that one view.

title: Redirect
what: {who} asked for {path} and Caddy sent it somewhere else (HTTP {status}).
why: A 308 is a permanent redirect, such as adding a trailing slash or moving from http to https. Normal.

title: Access log line (older format)
what: An older-format access log line: a request for {path} from {ip}, answered with HTTP {status}.
why: ALM used to show Caddy lines like this before it learned to write them as sentences.

title: {ip} banned
what: Fail2ban banned {ip}: its firewall rule now drops everything from that address.
why: {ip} crossed the failure threshold. The ban lasts for the jail's ban time, then lifts (you will see an 'unban' line).

title: Failed login counted against {ip}
what: Fail2ban saw a failed SSH login from {ip} and added it to that address's tally.
why: Fail2ban reads the SSH log and counts failures per address. Enough inside its time window and the address is banned.

title: Ban restored for {ip}
what: Fail2ban started up and put the existing ban on {ip} back in the firewall.
why: Bans live in fail2ban's own database so they survive a restart. This follows a fail2ban restart.

title: {ip} unbanned
what: The ban on {ip} expired and fail2ban removed its firewall rule.
why: Bans are temporary by design. If the address misbehaves again it will be banned again.

title: Fail2ban service lifecycle
what: Fail2ban was stopped, started or reported its state.
why: These appear when an admin restarts fail2ban to change its settings. Bans are restored afterwards.

what: {ip} used up its allowed login attempts as '{user}' and was cut off.
why: Classic brute force. sshd limits attempts per connection, and fail2ban counts the failures toward a ban.

title: Garbled SSH data
what: sshd received a packet from {ip} that did not check out (bad padding or a failed integrity check) and dropped the connection.
why: A broken client, a scanner sending junk, or a connection tampered with in transit. Isolated ones are noise.

title: Login session closed
what: The login session for {user} ended.
why: The other half of a 'session opened' line. Nothing to act on.

sig: sshd|pam_unix(sshd:session): session opened for user <user> by (uid=<n>)
title: Login session opened
what: A login session for {user} began.
why: PAM records every session start and end, so this pairs with a 'closed' line later.

sig: sshd|ssh_dispatch_run_fatal: Connection from <ip> port <n>: message authentication code incorrect [preauth]
title: Garbled SSH data
what: sshd received a packet from {ip} that did not check out (bad padding or a failed integrity check) and dropped the connection.
why: A broken client, a scanner sending junk, or a connection tampered with in transit. Isolated ones are noise.

title: Command run with sudo
what: {user} ran `{cmd}` as {as}, from {pwd}.
why: sudo logs every elevated command. If that was you, it is your audit trail. Commands that tail the Caddy or fail2ban logs come from ALM's follower.

title: sudo session closed
what: The sudo session for {user} ended.
why: The closing half of a sudo session.

sig: sudo|pam_unix(sudo:session): session opened for user <user> by (uid=<n>)
title: sudo session opened
what: A sudo session for {user} started.
why: sudo opens a short PAM session around each command.

title: Blocked packet, IP protocol {n}
what: UFW dropped a packet from {ip} that is neither TCP nor UDP (IP protocol number {n}; 1 is ICMP, the protocol behind ping).
why: The firewall is not answering these. Occasional ones are normal network chatter or scans.

title: Blocked TCP connection to port {n}
what: UFW, the firewall on myserver, dropped an unsolicited TCP connection attempt from {ip} to port {n}.
why: UFW logs every packet it blocks. Scanners across the internet probe ports around the clock, so a steady trickle is background noise. Eight or more from one address inside a minute is a port scan, and ALM raises its own error for that.

title: Blocked UDP packet to port {n}
what: UFW dropped an unsolicited UDP packet from {ip} to port {n}.
why: Same reason as a blocked TCP connection: nothing here is listening, so the firewall discards it. UDP probes are often looking for open DNS, NTP or game services.
